summary: The 1930s Bannerman Fire Tower in Fushimi Lake Provincial Park near Hearst; a 7 km trail reaches it, and Wikipedia says it remains fully intact.

access.note: Reached on the Fire Tower Trail inside Fushimi Lake Provincial Park, which the park describes as open to the public in summer for camping and day use. No source mentions a closure of the tower, and none says whether the tower itself can be climbed.

visit.trail_note: Fire Tower Trail: 7 km round trip, about two hours, strenuous; recommended for more advanced hikers

evidence.supports: Tower called the Bannerman Fire Tower; its cabin is the trail's main attraction
evidence.quote: The trail’s main attraction is the 1930s Bannerman Fire Tower and cabin.

evidence.supports: Tower built in the 1930s for forest fire detection (park blog)
evidence.quote: This hike highlights some of the history of Fushimi Lake, bringing you to the old fire tower that was built in the 1930s for forest fire detection.

evidence.supports: Tower constructed in the 1930s, on the north shore, within park boundaries
evidence.quote: A fire lookout tower , constructed in the 1930s, once operated on the north shore of Fushimi Lake within current park boundaries.

evidence.supports: Park is in Cochrane District, Ontario
evidence.quote: Fushimi Lake Provincial Park is a provincial park in Cochrane District , Ontario , Canada.

evidence.supports: Park is managed by Ontario Parks
evidence.quote: It is managed and staffed by Ontario Parks

evidence.supports: Structure described as steel; now disused but remains fully intact and standing
evidence.quote: The steel structure, now disused, remains fully intact as a prominent attraction for visitors, and one of the few examples of its kind still standing in the area.

evidence.supports: Towerperson watched the horizon for forest fires from May through September
evidence.quote: This trail transports you back to the 1930s, following the footsteps of the towerperson on his way to watch the horizon for forest fires from May through September.

evidence.supports: Trail passes the site of the cabin where a towerman and family would live
evidence.quote: Along the hike, you’ll pass the site of the fire ranger old cabin where a “towerman” and his family would live.

evidence.supports: Firelookout record names the site Sentier (Fushimi Lake); observer's cabin dilapidated, remains along the trail
evidence.quote: The dilapidated remains of the observer's cabin for this tower are located along the trail.

evidence.supports: Ontario Trails Council: one of the few original fire lookout towers left in Ontario
evidence.quote: This trail leads to one of the few original fire lookout towers left in Ontario.

evidence.supports: Fire Tower Trail is a strenuous 7 km hike of about two hours
evidence.quote: It’s a strenuous 7 km hike that can be completed in 2 hours.

evidence.supports: Fire Tower Trail is 7 km round trip; recommended for more advanced hikers
evidence.quote: The Fire Tower Trail is a recommended for more advanced hikers, as there are a few challenging spots on the 7 km round trip.

evidence.supports: One of the park's two hiking trails leads to a fire tower
evidence.quote: Two great hiking trails; one trail leads to a fire tower.

evidence.supports: Park open to the public in summer for camping and day-use
evidence.quote: Fushimi Lake is classified as an operating park, open to the public during the summer season for both camping and day-use recreation.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: firelookout.ca files the site as the Sentier (Fushimi Lake) Fire Tower; Ontario Parks calls the tower the Bannerman Fire Tower. Both describe a cabin along the trail to the tower, so the two names appear to refer to one site. The link rests on that shared detail, not on coordinates.

sources.title: It’s not a race: discovering the beauty of Fushimi Lake's trails
5 reasons to visit Fushimi Lake Provincial Park
Fushimi Lake Fire Tower Lookout Trail

notes_for_editor: Every source says only 'the 1930s' for the build date, so no built event is recorded (no year is documented). The firelookout.ca record ('Sentier (Fushimi Lake)') and the Ontario Parks pages ('Bannerman Fire Tower') are linked only by the cabin along the trail; the record's coordinates (49.84121, -83.87787) appear in no cited source, so the identity is an inference. Wikipedia's 'remains fully intact' comes from its own page; its cited reference [3] was not opened, so verify before publishing. The 'May through September' season is the park blog's wording, not a staffing record, so no staffing fact is recorded. Access: the sources describe a public trail in an open park but say nothing on whether the tower may be climbed; check with Ontario Parks before recommending the climb. A hobbyist list in the local cache also names a 'Fushimi Lake Tower' near Hearst as still standing, but its URL is not recorded in the cache, so it is not cited. The firelookout.ca record lists Structure Height and Year Built as N/A.
